captions: A bull bugles somewhere below the knob. High and thin, then a grunt like a man lifting something heavy.
The birds quit all at once, the way a room goes quiet when someone walks in.
Something screams up the drainage. Not an elk. Not a cat. It stops like a door closing.
Three knocks, wood on wood, out in the timber. Then three more, farther off. Answering.
Tracks circle the stones. Long, narrow, too far apart. They come to the edge of where the firelight was, and stop.
He bugles from close by, close enough to feel in your teeth. He is moving at last light. So is something else.
A stone the size of a fist drops into the coals. Sparks. Nothing moves out there. Then something does.
A stone cracks off a trunk a yard from your head. Thrown. From the dark, by something that can see you.
A branch breaks behind you. Big. Then the quiet that comes after something decides to stand still.
On the far ridge, against the last light, a shape stands where there was no tree this morning.
Two points of green at the edge of the firelight. Low, where a face would be. They do not blink. They go out.
The scream again. Closer. At the end it sounds like it is trying out a word.
A pale flash up on the knob. Your camera took something.
Knocks all around the camp now. Not answering each other. Counting.
Something walks the outside of the wall. You hear the logs take its weight and give it back.
It screams from right behind the wall. Your ears ring after.
More than one. The screams come from three places on the mountain, and then from one.
Stones rain into camp. One rings off the rifle barrel. They want you to run.
Two points of green in the timber, past the reach of the lamp. Level with your face, and higher than they should be. They do not blink. They go out.
Knocks in the timber all around you. Not answering each other. Counting. The fire is a long way off.
Something walks beside you, step for step, just outside the lamp. When you stop, it takes one more.
It screams from right behind you. Your ears ring after. When you swing the lamp there is only snow coming down.
Stones come out of the dark and crack off the trunks around you. One rings off the rifle barrel. They want you to run.
No birds. No wind. The whole mountain is holding its breath to see what you will do.
They are all around you now. Walk out, or stay and be kept.
Blank white park, black timber beyond. Branches. Snow sliding off needles.
Cows, feeding through at 02:14. Eyes like coins in the flash.
Empty. Then empty. Then empty.
Cows at 01:50, heads up, all looking the same way.
A faint smudge near the left edge. Dark, elongated, like a branch shadow that doesn't match any branch.
The next frame is clean.
At the edge of the frame, indistinct. Darker than the snow, roughly man-height.
Closer. Almost centred. Taller than any man.
Perfectly still, facing the lens. No detail. Just a shadow that has no business standing upright in an empty park.
Dry, light, snaps clean. Four of these will hold a fire till midnight.
The fire takes. Small. Enough.
You lay the fire in the stones: birch bark and dry grass for tinder, kindling, the four sticks set by. You will strike it when the light goes.
You lay the fire in the stones: birch bark, kindling, four sticks. Now the flint and steel.
The wall is up. Low, heavy, facing the timber. It will not stop what walks. It will make the walking have to choose.
You half-cut a dead spruce above the approach, wedge it, and run the cord back to your seat. Thirty feet of trunk waiting on one pull.
He drops in the frost and does not get up. The mountain goes quiet in a different register. The work is still ahead of you.
The shot is back. He humps into the timber and does not fall. Now you have a blood trail, and a problem.
The work is ugly and necessary. Quarters, backstraps, the heart. You leave the rest where the mountain can have it. The truck is the only direction that matters now.
You sit with your back to the stones and feed the fire. Sleep can wait until the dark has said what it came to say.
He gets your wind. A bark, a crash of timber, a rump going away. Wind on your neck is wind on his nose.
Your boots talk on the crust. He blows out of there and every ridge knows where you stood.
He sees you move. A long look, then he is gone in three jumps.
The bullet slaps wood. He is gone, and every ridge knows where you stood.
He is there, broadside. Then his head comes up. Not at you. At the timber behind you. He is gone in three jumps, and something in the timber screams where he was looking.
Blood on the snowberry, bright and frothy, then dark. He is hurt. He went this way.
Big tracks, last night's. He came through after dark and did not stop.
Beds dimpled deep in the snow, droppings in piles, saplings rubbed raw and polished dark. A seep steams at the upper end.
The snags talk in the wind. Elk paw through the ash for grass. Old rubs on the dead trunks.
Open water, steaming. Tracks come down to drink at first light, all of them pointed upslope after.
The duff is scuffed. Big beds under the spruce, still faintly warm in the middle. He lies up in here through midday.
From up here the park is a white page. Anything that moves on it, you will see.
Wind-scoured rock. The whole park below you, and the black timber around it.
Your boot tracks, the tent, the stones. Whatever else walked here walked carefully.
The trail forks. Blazes on the spruce, old axe marks gone grey.
The road. Tire tracks filling with snow. The way home.
Snow, and the quiet under it. You sit still long enough to hear your own blood.
Long, narrow prints, no claw marks. The stride too even, almost measured. Not crossing your trail. Following it.
A spruce snapped off above your head. The break is fresh and pale. Nothing fell on it.
Dark hair in the bark, long as your hand. Not deer. Not elk.
A pile in the snow, too big, grass and bone in it. It was warm this morning.
Wet earth and rot, hung in the cold air. Something stood here and breathed.

The truck ticks as it cools. The trail starts behind it, up through the spruce.
You set the flint and steel down. The fire is laid, waiting.
The Winchester lies across its tracks, stock gouged by something like teeth. It left it for you to find. That is worse.
Your hands go for the Winchester and find nothing. The Colt, then. Seven rounds and a short reach.
The magazine is empty. It is a heavy stick.
You power the camera down and sit a minute longer, scanning the park. Nothing moves. Old men see things, you think.
Glitch, you tell yourself. Cheap cameras do strange things in the cold.
Cows, coyotes, branches. Ordinary answers.
The crack rolls off three ridges and comes back to you smaller each time.
The .45 booms in the knoll. Muzzle flash in white strobes: bark-skin splintering, dark sap-like blood. It wrenches away downslope, breaking spruce like twigs.
The Winchester slams in the knoll. Muzzle flash in white strobes: bark-skin splintering, dark sap-like blood. It wrenches away downslope, breaking spruce like twigs.
You fire at the shape. It is not there when the flash clears. Something heavy goes away through the timber, not hurrying.
You hold it in the middle of what you can see. It steps behind a trunk. The trunk is empty.
You come to on your knees. The timber is empty. Your nerve is not.
You put the glass on it and wish the glass were empty. It is the height of a man stood on a man's shoulders. The arms hang wrong. It looks into the lens until you take it down.
It slams into you chest-high. One massive arm sweeps the rifle from your hands like a toy. Then it is gone into the spruce, the Winchester in one impossible hand. You have the Colt.
You moved. It is on you before you can turn: a smell of damp earth and rot, a weight like a falling tree. Then the timber is silent again.
Behind you, the timber breaks. Not stalking now. Coming. It wants what is on your back, or it wants you. The truck is close. RUN.
Behind you, the timber breaks. It has stopped pretending. The truck is close. RUN.
It hits you again and the world goes white. You are still on your feet. You do not know how.
A blow across the shoulders like a swung log. You go to your knees in the snow, and get up, because the truck is right there.
The second time you do not run. It loses interest in a man who will not bolt.
You keep the rifle down and the breath in your teeth. It passes. It may come again.
They are all around you now. Then one of them comes for the fire.
Branches break above camp, deliberate. Snow dumps from the high boughs. It is coming in.
You yank the cord. Thirty feet of trunk comes down across its shoulders with a sound like a shotgun. It roars for the first time. Shoot. Now.
It comes over the wall and through the fire like the fire is a rumor. You come to in the snow with the firelight on your face and the knoll empty.
The spur. Blazes on the spruce, old axe marks gone grey. Fresh tracks cut across the snow just past the post.
Cows, three of them, feeding along the edge of the park. No bull with them. Not yet. He is close: you can smell the rut on the wind. A camera on the saddle trail will tell you what moves at night.
Cows on the meadow, heads up, all looking at the timber.
Elk sign all over the park, but the bull is not showing himself. He moves at last light.
Nothing moving below. Wrong overlook, or he is somewhere you cannot see from here.

Elk. Prints wide as your palm, walking, not hurried. Cows, and one set bigger than the rest, sunk deep. They go down toward the park. You won't catch them on their tracks. Get high and let your eyes do the walking.
